The Flower Garden

Stories from the Ramayana

The Flower Garden

Rama and Sita meet in the flower garden

In everyday English — Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kanda

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is a gentle story. There is no war in it, no demon — only one morning, one flower garden, and two people seeing each other for the first time. Read it slowly, in a soft voice — as if you are walking among flowers.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Rama calm and slow, Sita shy and soft, her companions laughing.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The story of this book is from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kanda — Rama and Sita meeting in the flower garden before the contest of the bow. This is not Valmiki's telling — the difference is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya, archer. Warm dark-brown skin, a plain gold crown, no peacock feather. He has come to Mithila with his guru Vishvamitra.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, beside him at every step. Bow in hand, like Rama, a little lighter in complexion.

Sita — princess of Mithila, daughter of Janaka. Wheat-gold skin, long black braid with white jasmine flowers, small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on her left nostril, a deep red saree with a gold border, a small delicate gold tiara.

Sita's companions — the princess's friends, who come with her to the garden to pick flowers.

Vishvamitra — the great sage, guru of Rama and Lakshmana. White beard, saffron robes, kamandalu.

Janaka — king of Mithila, Sita's father. A middle-aged king, golden crown, royal robes.

Gauri — the goddess Parvati, whom Sita worships in the garden temple. Red saree with a gold border, calm and motherly in form.

1 · Rama Comes to Mithila · · RAMA COMES TO MITHILA

Rama and Lakshmana had come to Mithila with their guru Vishvamitra. Mithila — Janaka's city, where every lane smelled of flowers and every home sang songs of joy.

Janaka welcomed the sage and the two princes with great honour. He lodged them near a beautiful garden — a garden with beds of flowers, mango and Ashoka trees, and a small temple in the middle.

Everyone in the city knew — in Janaka's house lies the great bow of Shiva, and whoever lifts it and strings it shall be Sita's husband.

But the morning of the bow contest had not yet come. It was still a quiet evening — and the air of Mithila smelled of flowers.

Janaka said — “O sage, Mithila is blessed by your coming. Tomorrow morning there will be the contest of the bow — all the kings will come.”

Vishvamitra said — “O king, your city is beautiful — and the fame of your daughter Sita reaches far and wide.”

Rama said nothing. He looked quietly toward the garden — where flowers would bloom in the morning.

Pause and think — Rama is a guest in Mithila — he has seen neither the bow nor Sita yet. When we come to a new place, does our heart feel excitement — or peace? And why did Janaka lodge them near the garden — does staying near flowers also prepare the heart?

2 · The Flower Garden · · THE FLOWER GARDEN

Morning came. The first rays of the sun fell on the flowers of the garden — roses, champa, mogra, jasmine — all in bloom.

Rama and Lakshmana came into the garden to pick flowers. Flowers were needed for the guru's worship. The two brothers walked slowly between the flower beds — Rama ahead, Lakshmana behind, a basket of flowers in hand.

From the other side Sita too came into the garden — with her companions. She had come to pick flowers for the worship of Gauri. She too carried a basket of flowers, and jasmine flowers in her braid gave out their fragrance.

There were two parties in the garden — on one side Rama and Lakshmana, on the other Sita and her companions. Flowers on both sides, the quiet of morning on both sides — and flower beds in between.

(Read slowly here — the quiet of the garden should be heard.)

Pause and think — Both have come to pick flowers — one for worship, one for worship. Is picking flowers also part of worship? And the garden — does the heart grow quiet in a garden, as in a temple?

3 · The First Glance · · THE FIRST GLANCE

Then came that moment — whose story is sung even today.

Rama looked across the flower bed — and saw — Sita standing there, picking flowers. A red saree, a gold border, jasmine flowers in her braid — as if all the flowers of the garden had gathered in one place.

Sita too looked — across the bed stood two princes. One of them — dark, calm, a bow on his shoulder — as if the morning light of the garden had come walking.

Each looked at the other — and in each heart the same question rose — Who is this?

Rama asked Lakshmana softly — “Brother, who is this princess? I have never seen such beauty before.”

Lakshmana smiled and said — “Brother, this is Sita, daughter of Janaka — the one whose story we heard.”

Sita's companions too saw Rama — and laughed as they said to Sita — “Look, princess — what a prince has come!” — Sita lowered her eyes — and a soft blush came to her cheeks.

Nothing forceful happened — no promise, no noise. Only one glance — and a tender feeling woke in both hearts.

Pause and think — Rama and Sita only looked at each other — they did not even speak. Can just looking touch the heart? And the companions' laughter — can laughter sometimes tell a truth that the mouth does not say?

4 · Sita's Heart · · SITA'S HEART

Sita picked her flowers and returned from the garden — but her heart stayed behind in the garden.

On the way her companions kept talking of Rama — “How calm he is! What beauty! How the bow suits his shoulder!” — Sita listened quietly — she said neither yes nor no.

Back in the palace Sita arranged the flowers — but again and again the same image came before her eyes — the dark prince standing across the flowers.

Sita said in her heart — “Who is he? Can he be the one — of whom father said that whoever lifts the bow shall be my husband?”

A tender hope woke in Sita's heart — If only that Rama were my husband. — but she told this to no one — she kept it only in her heart.

Her companions understood — but they asked nothing either. They only smiled — as if to say — We understand, princess.

Pause and think — Sita told her hope to no one — she kept it only in her heart. Is it sometimes right to keep a matter of the heart in the heart? And the companions' smile — can someone understand another's heart without a word being spoken?

5 · The Prayer to Gauri · · THE PRAYER TO GAURI

Sita went to the small temple in the garden — where the image of Gauri stood. She offered flowers, lit a lamp — and prayed with folded hands.

Sita said to Gauri — “Mother Gauri, you know what is in everyone's heart. The hope that has woken in my heart — please fulfil it. May that same dark prince — Rama — be my husband.”

Sita said — “O Mother Gauri, I ask for nothing else — only grant me this boon, that Rama becomes my husband.”

The story says — Gauri was pleased. The garland of flowers on her image seemed to stir softly — and a quiet trust settled in Sita's heart — Mother has heard.

Sita opened her eyes — and smiled. Her heart grew light — as if it were filled with the fragrance of flowers.

(Read this in a whisper — as if it were a prayer.)

Pause and think — Sita asked Gauri for a boon — not wealth or a kingdom, only one person. Is it right to ask in prayer — or is prayer only for giving thanks? And the trust that Gauri was pleased — is trust itself also an answer to prayer?

6 · Rama's Heart · · RAMA'S HEART

Rama too had returned from the garden — but his heart too had stayed behind in the garden.

He said to Lakshmana — “Lakshmana, today in the garden I saw Janaka's daughter. My heart keeps going back to that side.” — Lakshmana smiled — “Brother, your heart never goes anywhere without reason.”

Rama also told his guru Vishvamitra what was in his heart — “Gurudev, today in the garden I saw Sita.” — Vishvamitra smiled — as if he already knew what was going to happen.

Vishvamitra said — “Rama, do not keep the matter of your heart only in your heart — tomorrow morning is the contest of the bow. What is to happen, will happen.”

Rama bowed his head — and fell silent. Now only one thing was in his heart — tomorrow morning. Tomorrow morning there would be the contest of the bow — and Sita would be there too.

Pause and think — Rama told what was in his heart to Lakshmana and to his guru — Sita told it only to Gauri. Does telling someone what is in your heart also take courage? And Vishvamitra's smile — does a guru sometimes already know what is in a disciple's heart?

7 · Toward the Bow · · TOWARD THE BOW

Night came. Lamps were lit in Mithila — and the whole city slept. But two hearts were awake — one in the palace, one near the garden.

As soon as morning came the city was astir — the day of the bow contest had arrived. In King Janaka's assembly hall lay the great bow of Shiva — heavy, huge, which no one had lifted for centuries.

All the kings would come — one by one they would try to lift the bow. And Rama would come too — with his guru.

Sita would be there too — seated beside her father, the wedding garland in her hand.

Sita said in her heart — “O Mother Gauri, what I asked yesterday — today is that day.”

Rama said in his heart — “Gurudev said — what is to happen, will happen.”

But this story — the story of the breaking of the bow — is not this book's. This book is only of that morning — when two people saw each other for the first time.

Pause and think — The morning of the bow contest has come — but this book stops here. Is the most beautiful part of a story sometimes the moment before what is going to happen? And Rama and Sita — both hold the same hope in their hearts — does one hope join two hearts?

8 · The Garden at Dawn · · THE GARDEN AT DAWN

That morning before the contest of the bow — the morning of the flower garden — was Mithila's gentlest morning.

The flowers bloomed again in the garden — as if nothing had happened yesterday. But the garden knew — yesterday two hearts had met here.

Rama and Sita — each had only looked at the other — they had not even spoken. But that one glance was enough — their hearts had met.

And Gauri had heard — Sita's prayer.

What happens next — the bow will break, the garland will be placed, the wedding will follow — that story is in the next book of this series.

Pause and think — This book begins not with war but with flowers — and stops before the bow. Is a love story also part of the Ramayana — as a war story is? And the garden — is a garden only a place of flowers — or also a place where hearts meet?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The story of this book is from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kanda, prakaranas 23–24 — Rama and Sita meeting in the flower garden (Pushpavatika) before the contest of the bow, and Sita's prayer to Gauri.

The Meeting in the Garden — Manas, Bal Kanda

Rama and Lakshmana coming into the garden to pick flowers; Sita coming with her companions to pick flowers for Gauri's worship; each seeing the other — this is in Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kanda.

The Prayer to Gauri — Manas, Bal Kanda

Sita worshipping Gauri in the garden temple and asking for Rama as her husband; Gauri pleased and granting her blessing — this is in Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kanda.

Kamban's Telling

The great poet Kamban of the south also tells, in his Ramayana (Kamba Ramayanam), of Rama and Sita meeting in the flower garden — there too the meeting happens before the contest of the bow.

The Difference from Valmiki — Please Read

It is important to know this — in Valmiki Ramayana there is no story of a meeting in the garden. In Valmiki, Rama sees Sita for the first time only after breaking the bow — when Janaka brings her into the assembly. The story of the first glance in the garden is Tulsidas's and Kamban's, not Valmiki's. This book tells that story — Tulsidas's and Kamban's telling, distinct from Valmiki's.

About the Contest of the Bow

The story of the bow contest and the wedding is not in this book — it is in the next book of this series. This book holds only the morning of the garden.

About the Pictures

The pictures of this book are kept tender — flowers, morning light, and looking from afar. Rama and Sita are shown sometimes near each other, sometimes looking toward each other — but never forcefully or boldly. A love story is told only with tenderness.
